q: How fast is CO2 in the atmosphere rising?

queries.purpose: Yearly rise in atmospheric CO2 at Mauna Loa, last 30 years
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(co2_ppm - LAG(co2_ppm) OVER (ORDER BY year), 2) AS value FROM co2_annual QUALIFY year >= (SELECT MAX(year) FROM co2_annual) - 29 ORDER BY year LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Average yearly rise in CO2 by decade
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(decade AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(diff), 2) AS value FROM (SELECT year, (year // 10) * 10 AS decade, co2_ppm - LAG(co2_ppm) OVER (ORDER BY year) AS diff FROM co2_annual) WHERE diff IS NOT NULL GROUP BY decade ORDER BY decade LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Annual mean CO2 level, every 5 years
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(co2_ppm, 1) AS value FROM co2_annual WHERE year % 5 = 0 OR year = (SELECT MAX(year) FROM co2_annual) ORDER BY year LIMIT 30

story.lead: CO2 in the air is rising about 2.7 ppm a year
story.summary: Carbon dioxide in the air is climbing faster than it used to. In the 1960s it rose by **0.86 ppm** a year on average; in the 2020s so far the average is **2.62 ppm** a year, about three times as fast. "ppm" means parts per million: a count of CO2 molecules in every million molecules of air. Measured at Mauna Loa in Hawaii, the yearly average reached **427.4 ppm** in 2025.
story.sub: Yearly average CO2 at Mauna Loa, Hawaii (NOAA), 1959–2025

facts.label: biggest rise in the last 30 years (2024)

points.h: Every recent year adds more than 1 ppm
points.p: Start with the last 30 years. In every one of them CO2 went up, never down. Yearly rises ranged from **1.14 ppm** in 1997 to **3.53 ppm** in 2024. The small rises sit near the start of this period, and the biggest ones are recent: 2016 (3.40) and 2024 (3.53). The latest year, 2025, added **2.74 ppm**.

points.h: Each decade has climbed faster than the last
points.p: Averaging by decade smooths out the ups and downs of single years. The pattern is clear: **0.86 ppm** a year in the 1960s, **1.64** in the 1980s, **2.40** in the 2010s and **2.62** in the 2020s so far. The only dip was in the 1990s, at 1.53, slightly below the 1980s. Apart from that, the speed of the rise has gone up decade after decade.

points.h: The total has gone from 317 to 427 ppm
points.p: These faster yearly rises add up. The yearly average was **316.9 ppm** in 1960 and **427.4 ppm** in 2025. That is a gain of about **110 ppm** in 65 years. Roughly half of it came in the last 25 years: from 369.7 in 2000 to 427.4 in 2025, a gain of about **58 ppm**. The level is higher, and it is also climbing faster.

story.takeaway: CO2 has risen in every one of the last 30 years, and the yearly rise has grown from under 1 ppm in the 1960s to more than 2.6 ppm now. That speed-up has pushed the average level from about 317 to 427 ppm.
story.note: Figures are yearly averages from one station in Hawaii, which is used as a measure of the global level.

story.lead: The United States and China tower over everyone
story.summary: The world's two biggest economies are far ahead of the rest. In 2023 the United States produced **$27.36 trillion** of goods and services, and China **$17.79 trillion**. Germany, in third place, managed only **$4.46 trillion**. Below, we look at the top 15, then at who is richest per person, and then at how the list looked in 2000.
story.sub: World Bank GDP and population data, current US dollars; mainly 2023, with 2000 for comparison.

facts.label: US economy in 2023, the world's largest

points.h: Two giants, then a long gap
points.p: Start with the size of each country's economy in 2023, measured in current US dollars. The United States leads with **$27.36 trillion**, and China follows with **$17.79 trillion**. China's economy is about four times Germany's **$4.46 trillion**. Japan (**$4.21 trillion**), India (**$3.55 trillion**) and the United Kingdom (**$3.34 trillion**) come next. By 15th place, Spain, the total is down to **$1.58 trillion**.

points.h: Big is not the same as rich per person
points.p: Size alone hides how well off the people in each country are. Dividing each economy by its population changes the order, for countries with over 10 million people. The United States still leads at **$81,249** per person, with Australia next at **$64,660**. China and India are not in the top 15 at all. Instead we find smaller economies like the Netherlands (**$62,545**) and Sweden (**$56,305**).

points.h: Go back to 2000 and China was sixth
points.p: Now look back to 2000 to see how much has moved. The United States was already first, at **$10.25 trillion**, so its economy has grown to about 2.7 times that size. China was sixth with **$1.21 trillion**, and its 2023 figure is nearly 15 times larger. Japan was a clear second in 2000 at **$4.97 trillion**, but by 2023 it had slipped to fourth at **$4.21 trillion**. These are current dollars, so part of the growth is rising prices.

story.takeaway: The United States and China are by far the largest economies, and no one else comes close. But the largest economies are not always the richest per person, and China's climb from sixth in 2000 to second in 2023 is one of the biggest changes in the ranking.
story.note: All figures are GDP in current US dollars, not adjusted for inflation; per-person figures only cover countries with over 10 million people.

q: How much has the world warmed?

queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(anomaly_c, 2) AS value FROM temperature WHERE source = 'GISTEMP' ORDER BY anomaly_c DESC LIMIT 10

story.lead: The world is about 1.3°C warmer than in the 1880s
story.summary: The planet's surface is clearly hotter than it was 140 years ago. NASA's records show the 2020s so far averaging **1.07°C** above the 1951–1980 average, while the 1880s sat **0.22°C** below it. That is a gap of about **1.29°C** between the first decade on record and the latest. The charts below show how the climb unfolded, how fast it has been lately, and which years top the list.
story.sub: NASA GISTEMP global surface temperatures, 1880–2025, compared with the 1951–1980 average.

facts.label: gap between the 1880s and the 2020s so far
warmest years are from 2015 or later

points.h: Each decade has been warmer than the last since the 1970s
points.p: Averaging by decade smooths out the ups and downs of single years. From the 1880s to the 1910s the world was slightly below the 1951–1980 average, at about **-0.2°C to -0.3°C**. Temperatures hovered near zero through the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s. Then the climb began: **0.25°C** in the 1980s, **0.59°C** in the 2000s and **1.07°C** in the 2020s so far. The steps have also grown, from about 0.14°C between the 1980s and 1990s to about 0.26°C between the 2010s and 2020s.

points.h: The last few years jumped above everything before
points.p: Zoom in on the last 30 years and the same rise shows up year by year. In 1996 the world was **0.33°C** above the old average, and by 2025 it was **1.19°C** above, a gain of 0.86°C. Not every year is warmer than the one before, as 2021 and 2022 dipped back to about 0.85°C and 0.89°C. But then 2023 reached **1.17°C** and 2024 hit **1.29°C**, higher than any year before 2023, when the peak had been 1.01°C.

points.h: The ten hottest years are all recent
points.p: Rank every year since 1880 and the top of the list is crowded with the latest ones. The three warmest are 2024 (**1.29°C**), 2025 (**1.19°C**) and 2023 (**1.17°C**). All ten warmest years are from 2015 or later, and the tenth place, 2018, is at 0.85°C. That is far above the decades of the early record, which sat below zero. So the warmth is not a one-off spike but a run of hot years.

story.takeaway: The world has warmed by roughly 1.3°C since the 1880s, measured against NASA's 1951–1980 yardstick. The warming has sped up in recent decades, and the very warmest years are all in the last eleven. 2024 is the hottest so far.
story.note: These figures compare with the 1951–1980 average, not with pre-industrial times, and the 2020s average covers only 2020–2025.

story.lead: US home prices are up about five-fold since 1987
story.summary: A typical US home now costs about **5.3 times** what it did in January 1987, a rise of **429%**. Since January 2000, prices have more than tripled. The climb was not smooth: there was a big boom, a fall of about a quarter, and a long recovery. West Coast cities rose the most, and the latest year has been almost flat.
story.sub: S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller home price index, January 1987 to July 2026, not adjusted for inflation.

facts.label: US national rise, January 1987 to latest month
San Diego's rise, the biggest of any area

points.h: A long boom, then a deep fall
points.p: The index sets January 2000 at 100, so 150 means prices are half as high again. In 1987 it stood at **66.3**. It crept up for years, then shot up in the 2000s to **183.5** in 2006, about 2.8 times the 1987 level. Then it turned: by 2011 it had dropped to **139.2**, a fall of about a quarter from the peak. By 2016 it was back to 180.9, close to the old high.

points.h: The West Coast pulled far ahead
points.p: The national rise hides big gaps between places. San Diego (**724%**), Portland (**714%**) and San Francisco (**696%**) rose the most, with Los Angeles and Seattle close behind. Dallas rose the least at **197%**, so San Diego's rise was about 3.7 times as big. The US as a whole, at **429%**, sits in the middle of the pack. Some cities have shorter records than 1987, for example Dallas starts in 2000, so each rise runs from that area's first month.

points.h: Since 2000, prices have more than tripled
points.p: Looking at each January shows how the story has played out lately. The index fell to **134.2** in 2012, then rose every year after that. It jumped from **212.4** in 2020 to **281.9** in 2022, a rise of about a third in two years. By January 2026 it reached **326.8**, about 2.4 times its 2012 low. But the last year was almost flat, up only about 1% from **323.6**.

story.takeaway: Over nearly four decades, US home prices have risen about five-fold, with a sharp fall in the middle. West Coast cities gained far more than the rest, and the national climb has now slowed to a near standstill.
story.note: Prices are in current dollars, not adjusted for inflation, so part of the rise just reflects higher prices across the economy.

story.lead: Oil prices rose fourfold, then swung wildly
story.summary: A barrel of Brent crude cost **$28.5** on average in 2000. By 2012 it cost **$111.7**, about four times as much. Since then the price has not settled: it halved in 2015, fell to **$41.8** in 2020, then climbed back above $100 in 2022. So far in 2026 it averages **$90.6**. All prices here are in current US dollars, not adjusted for inflation.
story.sub: Brent and WTI crude oil spot prices, US Energy Information Administration, 2000 to 2026 (2026 is a partial year), current US dollars per barrel.

facts.label: Brent's yearly average in 2020, the lowest since 2004
Highest single month for Brent, in 2008

points.h: A steady climb, then a crash, then more swings
points.p: Start with the yearly average. Brent stayed between **$24.5** and **$28.9** from 2000 to 2003, then climbed almost every year to **$96.8** in 2008. It dropped to **$61.5** in 2009 and recovered to **$111.3** in 2011. After four years between $99 and $112, the average fell to **$52.4** in 2015, about half the **$99** of 2014. Since then it has gone up and down between $41.8 and $100.8, and the 2026 average so far is $90.6.

points.h: The monthly peaks were far higher than the yearly averages
points.p: Averages hide the sharpest moments, so look at each year's most expensive month. The top came in 2008, when Brent reached **$132.7** in one month, well above that year's average of $96.8. Peaks of **$125.5** in 2012, **$123.3** in 2011 and **$122.7** in 2022 follow. In 2026 the highest month so far is **$117.3**, well above the peaks of 2023, 2024 and 2025, which were all under $94. This shows that a single month can sit far above the yearly average.

points.h: The US benchmark moved the same way, but sat lower
points.p: Is this only a Brent story? West Texas Intermediate (WTI), the main US benchmark, tells the same one. It rose from **$30.3** in 2000 to **$99.6** in 2008, fell to **$39.2** in 2020 and averages **$83.4** so far in 2026. In the early 2000s WTI was usually a little dearer than Brent. Since 2011 it has been cheaper in every year, with the biggest gap in 2012: **$94.1** against Brent's **$111.7**. The two prices rise and fall together, so the swings are real and not a quirk of one measure.

story.takeaway: Oil is far dearer than in 2000, but the path was bumpy, with peaks in 2008, 2011 to 2013 and 2022 and deep falls in 2009, 2015 and 2020. Both main benchmarks tell the same story. In 2026 prices are again high, and they have been unpredictable for most of this period.
story.note: Prices are in current US dollars, not adjusted for inflation, and 2026 covers only the months available so far.

story.lead: Yes, sea level is rising faster lately
story.summary: Seas have risen about **8.8 inches** (roughly 22 cm) between 1880 and 2010, and the pace has picked up. Tide-gauge records show the fastest decade yet in the 2000s, at **1.45 inches** per decade. Satellites then show an even quicker rise in 2013-2023, at **1.54 inches** per decade. Here are three views of the same story: the pace by decade, the satellite years, and the running total.
story.sub: Global average sea level: tide-gauge reconstruction (CSIRO) 1880-2013 and satellites (NOAA) 1993-2023, from US EPA data.

facts.label: Rise per decade in the 2000s (tide gauges)

points.h: The 2000s were the fastest decade on record
points.p: Start with the long tide-gauge record. The pace jumps around from one decade to the next: in the 1900s, 1920s and 1960s the sea barely moved, at about **0 inches** per decade. Most other decades added 0.55 to 0.85 inches, though the 1980s added only 0.14. But the 2000s stand out at **1.45 inches** per decade, the highest of all 13 decades. That is about two and a half times the 0.55 inches of the 1880s.

points.h: Satellites show the pace speeding up again
points.p: Satellites give a second, separate check from 1993. They measured **1.06 inches** per decade in 1993-2002 and **0.96** in 2003-2012, so the first two periods look alike. Then 2013-2023 jumped to **1.54 inches** per decade. That is about 45% faster than the first satellite period. These numbers are on a different baseline from the tide-gauge record, so compare the trends, not the totals.

points.h: Small yearly gains have added up to nearly nine inches
points.p: Add the decades together and you get the running total. By 1890 the sea had risen just 0.44 inches since 1880. By 2000 it was **7.06 inches**, and by 2010 **8.83 inches**. The 1.77 inches gained between 2000 and 2010 is about a fifth of the whole rise since 1880, packed into one decade out of 13. The total keeps growing, and it grows faster now than in the early records.

story.takeaway: Both records point the same way. The tide gauges show the fastest decade in the 2000s, and the satellites show the quickest recent stretch in 2013-2023. The sea is still rising, and the most recent decades have added more than earlier ones did.
story.note: The tide-gauge series ends in 2013 and the satellite series starts in 1993; they use different baselines, so they are not combined. Decade rates are fitted trends in inches per decade.

q: What is the US unemployment rate over time?

queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(unemployment_rate_pct), 1) AS value FROM us_employment WHERE year >= 1950 GROUP BY (year // 10) * 10 ORDER BY (year // 10) * 10 LIMIT 30

queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(employment_population_ratio_pct), 1) AS value FROM us_employment WHERE year >= 1950 GROUP BY (year // 10) * 10 ORDER BY (year // 10) * 10 LIMIT 30

story.lead: US unemployment has swung up and down for decades
story.summary: The share of Americans looking for work but not finding it has never stayed still. In the first 30 years shown, it ran from a low of **2.9%** in 1953 to **8.5%** in 1975. Averaged by decade, it was highest in the 1980s, at **7.3%**, and has been **4.8%** so far in the 2020s. Below, you can see the early ups and downs, then the long view by decade, and then how many people actually have a job.
story.sub: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, yearly averages 1947-2025; the first chart shows only 1947-1976.

facts.label: Average in the 1980s, the worst decade

points.h: Early years: calm stretches broken by sharp jumps
points.p: The chart shows the first 30 years, 1947 to 1976. Unemployment began at **3.9%** and fell to **2.9%** in 1953. A year later it was **5.5%**, so it can climb fast. It rose again to **6.8%** in 1958 and **6.7%** in 1961. By 1969 it was back down to **3.5%**. Then it reached **8.5%** in 1975, the highest in this stretch.

points.h: Each decade has usually been harder than the 1950s
points.p: Step back and average each decade, and the pattern is clearer. The 1950s averaged **4.5%** and the 1960s **4.8%**. The rate then rose to **6.2%** in the 1970s and peaked at **7.3%** in the 1980s. That is **2.8** points above the 1950s. It eased to **5.8%** in the 1990s and **5.5%** in the 2000s, rose to **6.2%** in the 2010s, and sits at **4.8%** so far in the 2020s.

points.h: But fewer people have jobs than in the 1990s
points.p: The jobless rate counts only people looking for work. Another measure asks how much of the whole population has a job. That share rose from **56.6%** in the 1950s to a peak of **62.8%** in the 1990s. It then fell to **59.3%** in the 2010s and **59.2%** in the 2020s. That is **3.6** points below the 1990s peak. So a modest unemployment rate in the 2020s sits alongside a smaller share of people working than in the 1990s.

story.takeaway: US unemployment does not drift. It jumps in some years and then falls back. The 1980s were the hardest decade on this measure, and the 2020s so far look much like the 1960s. The share of people with a job tells a different story, because it is lower now than in the 1990s.
story.note: Figures are yearly averages. The first chart shows only 1947 to 1976, while the decade charts cover 1950 to 2025, and the 2020s are 2020 to 2025 only.

queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(usd_per_ounce), 0) AS value FROM gold_prices WHERE year(month) >= 2000 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

story.lead: Gold now costs about 225 times its 1900 price
story.summary: An ounce of gold cost about **$19** in January 1900. In September 2026 it cost about **$4,319**, roughly **225 times** as much. Most of that jump came in two bursts: the 1970s, and the last few years. These figures are in current dollars, so some of the rise just reflects higher prices in general.
story.sub: Monthly gold prices in current US dollars per troy ounce, 1900 to September 2026 (2026 is a partial year).

points.h: For decades, gold barely moved
points.p: Look at gold by decade and the first surprise is how flat it was. The average price stayed between **$19** and **$36** an ounce from the 1900s through the 1960s. Then the 1970s average jumped to **$132**, and the 1980s reached **$418**. After a dip to **$351** in the 1990s, each decade has been higher than the one before, reaching **$2,453** so far in the 2020s.

points.h: Since 2000, the climb has sped up
points.p: Zoom in on the last quarter-century and the rise is steeper still. The yearly average went from **$279** in 2000 to **$1,670** in 2012. It then slipped to **$1,161** in 2015, so gold does fall as well as rise. The latest run is the sharpest: from **$1,943** in 2023 to **$3,442** in 2025 and **$4,552** so far in 2026.

story.lead: Coal is still the biggest source of CO2.
story.summary: Burning coal put out **15.8 billion tonnes** of CO2 in 2024, more than any other source. Oil came next at **12.5 billion tonnes**, then natural gas at **8 billion**. Together these three fuels make up almost all of the world's CO2 from fossil fuels and cement. Below, we look at today's mix, how coal's role has shrunk over a century, and how the total has grown.
story.sub: Global CO2 from fossil fuels and cement, Global Carbon Project, 1900-2024, shown as tonnes of CO2.

facts.label: Coal's share of CO2 in the 1900s

points.h: Coal leads, then oil and gas
points.p: Start with the latest full year, 2024. Coal gave **15.8 billion tonnes** of CO2, oil **12.5 billion** and natural gas **8 billion**. Cement added **1.5 billion** and burning off gas at oil wells added **0.4 billion**. So three fuels account for nearly all of it, and coal is the largest by a clear margin.

points.h: Coal once ruled, now holds about 40%
points.p: Coal has not always shared the lead. In the 1900s it caused **95%** of the CO2 counted here. That share fell steadily to **35.2%** in the 1970s as oil and gas grew. It then rose again, to **41.3%** in the 2010s and **40.9%** so far in the 2020s. Coal is no longer the only source, but it is still the biggest.

points.h: The total is now about 15 times bigger
points.p: A smaller share for coal did not mean less CO2 overall. Yearly emissions averaged **2.4 billion tonnes** in the 1900s. They reached **11.2 billion** in the 1960s and **35.4 billion** in the 2010s. For 2020-2024 the average is **37.2 billion tonnes**, about 15 times the 1900s level. Growth in the last decade has been much slower than in earlier ones, but the total is still at its highest.

story.takeaway: Most of the world's CO2 comes from burning coal, oil and gas, with coal still on top at about 40%. Coal's dominance of a century ago has faded, but the total has grown so much that coal alone now gives far more CO2 than all sources did in 1900.
story.note: These figures cover CO2 from fossil fuels and cement only, converted from tonnes of carbon to tonnes of CO2. The 2020s average covers 2020-2024.

By 1960 the glaciers had lost **2.0 metres**, by 1990 **8.3 metres**, and by 2023 **29.7 metres**. At every five-year mark the total is higher than at the one before. story.lead: Late 2008 was the stock market's most volatile stretch
story.summary: The wildest month for the US stock market since 1990 was October 2008, when the "fear index" (the VIX) closed at **59.9**. That is more than five times the calm level of 2017, when the yearly average was **11.0**. Six of the twelve scariest months on record fall between October 2008 and March 2009. Below, we look at the peaks, then the yearly averages, then the decades.
story.sub: Monthly closing values of the VIX, January 1990 to September 2026; yearly chart covers 1990–2019.

facts.label: Top fear months that fall in Oct 2008–Mar 2009

points.h: The financial crisis holds the top spots
points.p: The VIX is a fear gauge: the higher it goes, the more investors expect wild swings in stocks. Its highest month ever was October 2008 at **59.9**, followed by November 2008 at **55.8**. Then comes March 2020 at **53.5**, the first month of the pandemic. Six of the twelve highest months are in the winter of 2008–09, so the fear lasted for months rather than a single scare. The rest of the list is February 2020 (40.1), two months in 1998 (44.3 and 41), one in 2002 and one in 2011.

points.h: Calm years and nervous years alternate
points.p: Single peaks can mislead, so the yearly averages show which years were jumpy overall. Among the years 1990–2019, 2009 (**31.8**) and 2008 (**31.6**) were the most nervous, with 2002 (26.6) and 1998 (26.2) next. The quietest year was 2017, at **11.0**, which is nearly three times lower than 2008. Calm stretches also appear, such as 1992–1995 and 2004–2006, when the average stayed near 12 to 15. This chart stops at 2019, so it does not show the 2020s.

points.h: Decade by decade, the 2000s were the jumpiest
points.p: Averaging by decade smooths out single years. The 2000s were the most volatile at **21.9**, which includes the 2008 crisis and the 2002 spike. The 2010s were the calmest at **17.1**, with the 1990s in between at 18.5. The 2020s are already up to **20.7**, counting months up to September 2026. That is close to the 2000s, but it is not a full decade yet.

story.takeaway: Fear in the stock market peaked in the financial crisis of 2008–09, both in the single highest month and in the yearly averages. March 2020 came close for one month, but it did not last as long. Calm years like 2017 show how far apart the quiet and stormy times can be.
story.note: The VIX figures are monthly closing values, so a wilder day within a month could be hidden. The 2020s average includes months only up to September 2026.

story.lead: US rates climbed to 1981, then fell for decades.
story.summary: The interest rate on 10-year US government loans rose for three decades, then fell for nearly four. In the 1950s it averaged **3.24%** a year. By the 1980s it was **10.59%**, more than three times as high. Since then it has come back down, to **2.41%** in the 2010s. Here is how that rise and fall played out.

points.h: Up for thirty years, then down for forty
points.p: Start with the big picture, decade by decade. The average yield went from **3.24%** in the 1950s to **4.67%** in the 1960s and **7.5%** in the 1970s. It peaked in the 1980s at **10.59%**. After that each decade was lower than the one before: **6.66%** in the 1990s, **4.46%** in the 2000s and **2.41%** in the 2010s. The 2020s, at **3.1%**, are the first decade to break that pattern with a rise.

points.h: From 1990, a long and bumpy slide
points.p: Zoom in on the years since 1990 and the slide is clear. The yearly average started at **8.55%** in 1990 and dropped to about **4%** by 2003, at **4.01%**. It fell further to **1.8%** in 2012, the lowest year on this chart. There were pauses along the way, such as a jump from **5.87%** in 1993 to **7.08%** in 1994. By 2019 the rate was **2.14%**, about a quarter of its 1990 level.

points.h: The peak: the early 1980s
points.p: How high did rates ever go? The ten highest years are all from 1979 to 1990. The top year was 1981 at **13.91%**, followed by 1982 at **13%** and 1984 at **12.44%**. Compared with **1.8%** in 2012, the lowest year from 1990 to 2019, the 1981 peak was nearly eight times higher. So today's rates are far below the early-1980s extreme, though above the lows of the 2010s.

story.takeaway: US long-term interest rates rose until the early 1980s and then fell for about thirty years. The 2020s average is a little above the 2010s, but still far below the peak.

story.lead: Natural gas is cheaper than usual, but not at its lowest
story.summary: The latest price, for August 2026, was **$2.78** per million BTU (a standard unit of energy). That is about a third below the average of **$4.09** since 1997, and below the typical month at **$3.40**. But it is well above the cheapest month on record, **$1.49** in March 2024. Here is how the last two years, the long run and the extremes fit together.
story.sub: Henry Hub natural gas spot price (US EIA), monthly, January 1997 to August 2026, in nominal US dollars per million BTU.

facts.label: Price in August 2026, per million BTU

points.h: After a winter spike, prices have settled near $3
points.p: Over the last two years, prices have mostly moved between **$2** and **$4**. They climbed to **$4.26** in December 2025, then jumped to **$7.72** in January 2026, the highest in this stretch. By February they were back to **$3.62**. Since April 2026 every month has been between **$2.77** and **$3.15**, so August's **$2.78** is the low end of that calm run.

points.h: Seen year by year, today looks fairly ordinary
points.p: Zoom out and the recent price looks less dramatic. Yearly averages reached **$8.81** in 2005 and **$8.86** in 2008, and **$6.42** in 2022. They fell as low as **$2.03** in 2020. The 2026 average so far is **$3.61**, a little above 2025's **$3.53** and well above 2024's **$2.19**. The latest month sits below that 2026 average, because the January spike pulls it up.

points.h: Cheaper than typical, but far from the bottom
points.p: Put the latest month beside the extremes and its place is clear. At **$2.78** it is below both the average (**$4.09**) and the median (**$3.40**). The median is the middle month: half of all months cost less, half more. It is still almost double the record low of **$1.49**. It is also about a fifth of the peak of **$13.42** in October 2005. Gas is cheap by the long-run measure, not at rock bottom.

story.takeaway: Natural gas now costs less than in a typical month since 1997, and far less than in its expensive years. It is not the cheapest it has been, and winter has shown it can jump quickly. These are nominal dollars, so part of the long-run gap simply reflects inflation.
story.note: Prices are in current US dollars, not adjusted for inflation, and 2026 covers January to August only.

story.lead: Lebanon has the highest recent inflation, by far.
story.summary: In 2023, prices in Lebanon rose **221.3%**. That means prices were about **3.2 times** their level a year earlier. No other country with recent figures comes close, though Sudan (**138.8%** in 2022) and Zimbabwe (**104.7%** in 2022) were also very high in their last reported years. Below, we look at the latest figures, then a single year (2023) so countries are fairly compared, then the worst years on record since 1960.
story.sub: World Bank yearly consumer price inflation, 1960–2024; recent charts use each country's latest year from 2022 on.

facts.label: Lebanon's price rise in 2023, the highest recent figure
Sudan's price rise in 2022, its last year of data
Congo (Dem. Rep.) in 1994, the highest on record

points.h: Lebanon leads, with Sudan and Zimbabwe behind
points.p: Take each country's most recent figure from 2022 onward, and Lebanon is on top with a **221.3%** rise in 2023. Sudan comes next at **138.8%** and Zimbabwe at **104.7%**, but both only have figures up to 2022. Turkiye follows at **58.5%** in 2024, and Iran, Haiti, Egypt, Malawi and Ethiopia all sit between 30% and 45%. Every country in this top 15 saw prices rise by more than a fifth in its latest year, so the gap to the top three is large.

points.h: Compare the same year and Lebanon still stands alone
points.p: The first list mixes different years, so here is 2023 alone, when nearly every country has a figure. Lebanon is still first at **221.3%**, about **four times** Turkiye in second place at **53.9%**. Suriname (**51.6%**) and Sierra Leone (**47.6%**) are close behind Turkiye. Sudan and Zimbabwe drop out because they have no figures after 2022. Even so, the 15th country, Sao Tome and Principe, saw prices rise **21.3%** in one year.

points.h: Today's worst is mild next to the record years
points.p: Go back to 1960 and today's numbers shrink. The Democratic Republic of the Congo hit **23,773%** in 1994, which means prices rose to roughly **238 times** their level a year before. Bolivia reached **11,750%** in 1985 and Peru **7,482%** in 1990. All 15 of these record years fall between 1966 and 1997, and none is recent. Lebanon's 2023 rise is large, but the Congo's 1994 peak is about **107 times** bigger.

story.takeaway: Lebanon has the highest inflation in the latest data, with Sudan, Zimbabwe and Turkiye also high. But the worst episodes on record, mostly in the 1980s and 1990s, were far more extreme than anything seen recently.
story.note: Coverage is uneven: Sudan and Zimbabwe end in 2022, and 2024 has fewer countries, so the first chart mixes years shown in each label.

story.lead: Los Angeles, Miami and San Diego led the rise
story.highlight: Los Angeles, Miami and San Diego
story.summary: Home prices in Los Angeles are up **353%** since January 2000, so a home that cost 100 then would now cost about 453. Miami (**352%**) and San Diego (**350%**) are almost level with it. Even Detroit, at the bottom of this top-20 list, has seen prices climb **104%**, or roughly double. The charts below show who led over 26 years, who led over the last 10, and who is rising fastest now.

Miami's rise over the last 10 years

points.h: Three California and Florida giants lead the long climb
points.p: Start with the long view, from January 2000 to now. Los Angeles (**353%**), Miami (**352%**) and San Diego (**350%**) are in a near three-way tie at the top. Seattle (**293%**), Tampa (**274%**) and San Francisco (**271%**) follow some way behind. Further down, Chicago (**137%**), Cleveland (**111%**) and Detroit (**104%**) have risen much less, but prices there still more than doubled.

points.h: Over ten years, Florida and the Sun Belt pull ahead
points.p: Narrow the window to the last ten years and the order changes. Miami is first at **111%**, with Tampa and Charlotte next at **105%** each, and Phoenix at **103%**. Los Angeles drops to 13th place with **82%**. San Francisco (**62%**) and Washington (**59%**) are at the bottom of this list. So the long-run leaders are not all recent leaders: Miami stays near the top, but Los Angeles does not.

points.h: In the last five years, Miami still leads, and others catch up
points.p: The last five years tell a third story. Miami is still first with **49%**, followed by New York (**46%**) and Chicago (**43%**). Chicago ranked 18th over the long run, so this is a big move up. Seattle (**15%**), Denver (**14%**), Portland (**12%**) and San Francisco (**11%**) have risen the least in this period. Miami is the only city in the top three of all three charts.

story.takeaway: Which city is the biggest winner depends on the time frame. Los Angeles, Miami and San Diego lead since 2000, while Miami leads over both ten and five years. Cities such as Chicago, Detroit and Cleveland, which lagged over the long run, have been rising faster lately.
story.note: The index is not adjusted for inflation, and most cities' latest month is June 2026. The 10-year and 5-year rises are measured from the same month in earlier years.
